item.content:encoded:
What’s in store for VMware Explore 2026 in Las Vegas?

Well, content is always top-of-mind for attendees and we are thrilled to present more than 350 technical sessions this year, brought to the stage by a wide array of expert speakers. From Community Quick Talks to deep dives on the new VMware Cloud Foundation 9.1, there’s no shortage of ways to stay busy at Explore. Read on for a sneak peek of a few of this year’s featured sessions and add them to your agenda today!

REGISTER NOW

Plenary Session [PLE1837LV]

Monday, August 31 | 4:00 – 5:00 PM PDT

Get ready to hit ‘snooze’ on that Tuesday morning alarm. Now on Monday afternoon, join us for a spotlight session hosted by Broadcom leaders and experts to learn more about the future of the data center in an era of AI and rapid innovation, included only with the Full Event Pass.

PRO-TIP Wishlist vs. Scheduled: Favoriting a session is not reserving a seat. First log in with a free account, then click “Add to Schedule” on the session listing. 

A Deep Dive: What’s New for VMware vSphere in VMware Cloud Foundation 9.1 [CLOB1082LV]

Tuesday, September 12:00 – 2:45 PM PDT

Discover the latest VMware vSphere innovations powering VMware Cloud Foundation (VCF) 9.1. This session explores key technology updates, performance improvements, and management simplifications impacting daily operations. Through demonstrations and real-world examples, you will see how these changes improve workload efficiency, reduce complexity, and strengthen infrastructure. Whether you are planning an upgrade, evaluating features, or staying current, this session delivers essential technical depth and practical insights.

item.title: The Odyssey Tournament is back at VMware Explore 2026
item.dc:creator: david dentremont
item.description:
Odyssey has a way of turning a conference trip into something you talk about for years. The competition is back at VMware Explore 2026 in Las Vegas, and if you missed it before, this is the year to show up ready to play. Whether you’re there to win or just to see what the best … Continued

The post The Odyssey Tournament is back at VMware Explore 2026 appeared first on VMware Blogs.
item.content:encoded:
Odyssey has a way of turning a conference trip into something you talk about for years. The competition is back at VMware Explore 2026 in Las Vegas, and if you missed it before, this is the year to show up ready to play.

Whether you’re there to win or just to see what the best in the room can do, Odyssey delivers. Complete technical challenges using VMware software, climb the leaderboard, and if you crack the top 8, walk away with serious prizes. Everyone who plays gets something. More on that below.

How it works

Stop by the Odyssey stage inside the Hands-on Labs room at The Venetian Convention and Expo Center, August 31 through September 2, 2026. Play the qualifying games Monday and Tuesday. Tasks are scored on accuracy and speed, so knowing your stuff and moving fast both matter. Bonus points go to players who finish fastest.

The top 8 scores across all three daily rounds advance to the live finals on Wednesday, September 2 at 11am. That’s when the leaderboard stops being a number and starts being a story.

What you take home

You don’t have to finish in the top 8 to leave with something. Everyone who plays a game receives an Odyssey keychain charm to add to your official collection* and while supplies last, an Odyssey pin. You’ll also pick up electronic tokens redeemable in the Explore Expedition game, accessible through the Explore Mobile App.
*Be sure to get your official VCF Keychain from the VMware booth in the HUB first!

The top 8 finishers each take home an Odyssey Yeti water bottle and receive an Odyssey Letterman Jacket. The jacket has been a fan favorite since the earliest tournaments, and this year’s version is worth competing for.

And the top 3? Fantastic Lego sets. The kind worth clearing shelf space for before you travel.

The live finals

The finals are worth attending even if you’re not on the leaderboard. Top players take on live technical challenges in front of the crowd, and the pressure is real. Lead changes happen right up until the end, and past tournaments have kept spectators on their feet until the final result. If you want to see VMware technical skill at its sharpest in a live setting, Wednesday, September 2 at 11am the Odyssey stage is where to be.

Hands-on Labs tours

Odyssey is also part of the Hands-on Labs tours running throughout the event. These behind-the-scenes tours take you through the entire Hands-on Labs room with the engineers and product specialists who built what you’re learning — business context, technical depth, and a look at the Command Center that monitors the lab environment in real time. Tours run approximately 30 to 45 minutes and are available to all attendees.

Hands-on Labs, for everyone

Not every experience at Explore 2026 needs to be competitive. The Hands-on Labs area covers cloud, security, and AI through Self-paced Labs and Expert-led Workshops. Labs are built for all experience levels — move at your own pace and ask questions without a clock running.

Workshop sessions run smaller and tighter, with direct access to the people who built the content. If you’re newer to the VMware portfolio, these labs give you practical, hands-on familiarity with the tools before you’re expected to use them in production. If you’ve been working with VMware software for years, the challenge content will find your ceiling.

Register and get on the leaderboard

Odyssey seats are limited. If competing is on your agenda, register for VMware Explore 2026 now and plan to stop by the Hands-on Labs room on day one.

Register here

VMware Explore 2026 runs August 31 through September 3 at The Venetian Convention and Expo Center in Las Vegas, Nevada. See you there.

item.title: Introducing the VCF Inspector Fling: A Standalone Diagnostic and Health Tool for VMware Cloud Foundation 9.1
item.dc:creator: vmwareblogs
item.description:
We are excited to announce the VCF Inspector fling, a new standalone diagnostic, health inspection, and troubleshooting tool built specifically for VMware Cloud Foundation (VCF) 9.1 and VCF management services. The VCF Inspector fling gives infrastructure administrators, support engineers, and solution architects instant, structured visibility into VCF 9.1 environments without requiring manual command-line troubleshooting, custom … Continued

The post Introducing the VCF Inspector Fling: A Standalone Diagnostic and Health Tool for VMware Cloud Foundation 9.1 appeared first on VMware Blogs.
item.content:encoded:
We are excited to announce the VCF Inspector fling, a new standalone diagnostic, health inspection, and troubleshooting tool built specifically for VMware Cloud Foundation (VCF) 9.1 and VCF management services.

The VCF Inspector fling gives infrastructure administrators, support engineers, and solution architects instant, structured visibility into VCF 9.1 environments without requiring manual command-line troubleshooting, custom SSH scripting, or deploying heavy virtual appliances.

The VCF Inspector fling is available today as a free download on the Broadcom Support Portal under VMware Flings here.

Why We Built VCF Inspector

Introduced in VCF 9.1, VCF management services provides a unified architecture for centralized lifecycle and operational management across the entire VCF fleet. It hosts key fleet and instance-level services including lifecycle management services, VCF SSO, Log Management, Salt configuration management, and more.

While this unified model delivers streamlined lifecycle operations and global visibility, managing and troubleshooting through VCF Operations, these interconnected services require inspecting component health, platform certificates, interconnects, and lifecycle workflows as an integrated platform.

To empower administrators and accelerate operational confidence, the VCF Inspector fling addresses three key use cases:

  1. Proactive Pre-Upgrade Readiness: Giving admins an automated, single-click method to verify password policy compliance, host readiness, network reachability, and certificate validity before initiating a VCF 9.1 upgrade
  2. Streamlined Deployment and Upgrade Visibility: Delivering real-time, consolidated timeline progress for VCF installations and upgrades, giving teams clear visibility into subtask execution and automatic root-cause guidance without manual log searching across control plane nodes
  3. Instant Day-2 Runtime Diagnostics: Providing structured, instant health inspection across all platform services, making it easy to monitor service states, restart trends, and relevant Knowledge Base recommendations from a unified interface

The VCF Inspector fling delivers all three capabilities in a single executable designed to run on your admin workstation or a jumpbox.

Key Capabilities and Use Cases

The VCF Inspector fling supports three core use cases out of the box:

1. VCF 9.1 Pre-Upgrade Readiness Assessment

Now you don’t need to be an expert on the VCF documentation or understand every Knowledge Base (KB) article. Run multiple automated pre-flight checks against SDDC Manager and vCenter before initiating a VCF upgrade. The tool validates:

  • Password policy compliance and account expiration dates
  • Host health and vSphere cluster readiness
  • Required network port reachability (SSH 22, HTTPS 443, Platform API 5480, Cluster API 6443)
  • Active lifecycle management task status and certificate expiration thresholds
  • Surfacing actionable remediation guidance for failed checks

Pre-checks

2. Live Deployment and Upgrade Timeline Monitor

Track ongoing VCF installation or upgrade progress in real-time. Features include:

  • Real-time timeline view of SDDC Manager subtasks and Bootstrap stages
  • Automatic stuck-task detection and root-cause error extractions
  • Direct deep-links to Broadcom KB articles for known deployment issues
  • Stage duration calculation and stage filtering
  • Enhanced monitoring of deployment tasks for VCF management services

Detailed VCF Management Services tasks

3. Day-2 VCF Management Services Health and Diagnostics

Inspect the health of all running platform services with zero configuration:

  • Instant Service Health: Grouped view of VCF management services (log management , fleet lifecycle, VCF Automation, identity broker, VMware Salt for VCF components, telemetry) with health badges
  • Platform IP and FQDN Pool Discovery: Comprehensive datagrid mapping Control Plane VIPs, Worker Node IPs, canonical FQDNs, and LoadBalancer services
  • Node Topology Grid: Visual matrix of Control Plane and Worker nodes displaying component placement and status
  • Log Analyzer and Component Diagnostics: Mine recent error and warning log patterns across platform services, with instant component diagnostics and execution logs in a detail modal
  • Administrative Remediation Actions: One-click cert-manager certificate renewal, DNS rolling restart, system database compaction, and network reachability testing—protected by an interactive safety acknowledgment lock
  • Safe Terminal Console: Advanced user console with strict read-only command validation, allowing safe status queries while blocking destructive operations

VCF Management Services overview

Remediation actions and controlled console

Advanced troubleshooting

How to Get Started

Getting started with the VCF Inspector fling takes minutes:

  1. Download the Binary: Visit the Broadcom Support Portal – Free Downloads / VMware Flings and download the single binary for your operating system (vcf-inspector-darwin-arm64-native, vcf-inspector-windows-amd64-native.exe, or vcf-inspector-linux-amd64).
  2. Make Executable and Launch:
    • macOS/Linux: Open Terminal, run chmod +x ./vcf-inspector-darwin-arm64-native, and run ./vcf-inspector-darwin-arm64-native.
    • Windows: Double-click vcf-inspector-windows-amd64-native.exe.
  3. Connect to Your Environment:
    • Enter the IP or FQDN of any VCF control plane node (or SDDC Manager).
    • Provide the vmware-system-user credentials (or SDDC Manager admin credentials).
    • The VCF Inspector fling establishes a secure session and populates all health dashboards automatically.

Summary and Feedback

The VCF Inspector fling streamlines VCF 9.1 troubleshooting into a single, elegant tool that requires zero installation or infrastructure footprint. Whether you are prepping for a VCF 9.1 upgrade, monitoring an active deployment, or performing day-2 health checks, The VCF Inspector fling gives you the insights you need instantly.

Try out the VCF Inspector fling today, and share your feedback, bug reports, and feature requests with us via the VMware Flings community channels!

item.title: Modernizing Infrastructure: VMware Cloud Foundation 9.0.x to 9.1 Upgrade Guide
item.dc:creator: vmwareblogs
item.description:
With the release of VMware Cloud Foundation (VCF) 9.1, private cloud maturity has entered a highly programmatic, scalable era. Moving your infrastructure into this release represents more than a routine software lifecycle step, it is a transition into a modernized, modular architecture. Upgrading to VCF 9.1 eliminates the overhead of managing separate appliances for Lifecycle … Continued

The post Modernizing Infrastructure: VMware Cloud Foundation 9.0.x to 9.1 Upgrade Guide appeared first on VMware Blogs.
item.content:encoded:
With the release of VMware Cloud Foundation (VCF) 9.1, private cloud maturity has entered a highly programmatic, scalable era. Moving your infrastructure into this release represents more than a routine software lifecycle step, it is a transition into a modernized, modular architecture.

Upgrading to VCF 9.1 eliminates the overhead of managing separate appliances for Lifecycle Manager, during the transition, the existing environment appliances are automatically decommissioned, and their core capabilities are streamlined into a modern, single-appliance architecture.

For VCF 9.0 users, version 9.1 introduces a unified Management Services layer. 
We highly recommend checking out our VCF 9.1 Announcement Blog for a deep dive into the new features and licensing model.

Ready to make the jump? This post breaks down exactly how to do it, anchored by a comprehensive, step-by-step upgrade demo.

What’s New

The fleet management and critical control operations were distributed across various separate standalone virtual appliances. VCF 9.1 completely centralizes these functions into a single runtime layer.

The primary structural shift when jumping from VCF 9.0.x to 9.1 involves:

  • Consolidating into VCF Operations.
  • Bootstrapping the VCF Management Services Cluster, VCF 9.1 introduces VCF Management Services to provide a unified architecture for centralized lifecycle and operational functionalities. The services runtime of the initial VCF instance hosts the fleet-level components responsible for global operations, alongside its own instance-level components. Additionally, every VCF instance includes a dedicated services runtime that hosts instance-level management services for executing local tasks.

Architectural Guardrails: Planning for Success

VCF 9.1 introduces a high degree of configuration validation to ensure smooth upgrade of the environment. Before staging any installation payloads, ensure your pre-upgrade environment meets these strict criteria:

  • Strict DNS and Case Sensitivity: VCF 9.1has an improvement in checks with absolute network precision. All existing and new network assignments must utilize strictly lowercase Forward and Reverse DNS records to prevent switchover validation errors.
  • Pre-allocated Network Staging: One must pre-allocate dedicated static IP addresses and map Forward/Reverse DNS entries for your new VCF Management Services (configured as an IP Pool using strict CIDR notation in the UI) and the headless VCF License Server.
  • Backups: Backing up your VMware Cloud Foundation (VCF) environment requires configuring both native file-based backups for vCenter and SFTP targets for SDDC Manager and VCF Operations(Imaged Based backup).

Visualizing the 9.1 Upgrade

While understanding the high-level milestones is essential for architectural planning, seeing the interface interactions and validation checks in real time makes execution much easier.

To see this entire upgrade workflow in action including a deep dive into the deployment screens, data migrations, and live cluster bootstrapping watch our full video walkthrough below:

VCF 9.0.x to VCF 9.1 – Upgrade Video – Part 1

VCF 9.0.x to VCF 9.1 – Upgrade Video – Part 2

Scope of the Environment

The transition to VCF 9.1 requires a highly orchestrated lifecycle sequence. The table below outlines the specific scope of the environment and the upgrade phases mapped to this 9.0.x to 9.1 evolutionary path.

This orchestrated transition ensures that your entire stack from operations and control planes down to the underlying compute and networking fabric moves uniformly to the 9.1 runtime baseline. For any product components not listed above, please refer to this link.
Upgrading to VMware Cloud Foundation 9.1

Conclusion: Bringing it All Together

The move to VCF 9.1 is a strategic step toward a programmatic, scalable private cloud. By following the 8-step orchestrated sequence and accounting for the new architectural guardrails like the VCF Management Services layer and refined password standards, customers can transition from 9.0.x with confidence.

Ready to start your transition? Consult the VCF 9.1 Release Notes and verify your hardware against the latest HCL to ensure a future-ready foundation.

item.title: Memory Tiering for VMs and VKS: Deployment Flexibility, Smarter Consolidation, Intelligent Resource Consumption
item.dc:creator: vmwareblogs
item.description:
If you’re running workloads on vSphere Kubernetes Service (VKS) today, or planning to, one of the questions that comes up quickly is how container workloads interact with infrastructure-level capabilities like Memory Tiering. Can VKS take full advantage of the same memory efficiency features that VM workloads use? Does adding a Kubernetes layer on top change … Continued

The post Memory Tiering for VMs and VKS: Deployment Flexibility, Smarter Consolidation, Intelligent Resource Consumption appeared first on VMware Blogs.
item.content:encoded:
If you’re running workloads on vSphere Kubernetes Service (VKS) today, or planning to, one of the questions that comes up quickly is how container workloads interact with infrastructure-level capabilities like Memory Tiering. Can VKS take full advantage of the same memory efficiency features that VM workloads use? Does adding a Kubernetes layer on top change the performance story? We’re glad you’ve asked, because we put it to the test, and the results are worth talking about.

What we want to walk you through today is how VKS, running natively inside VMware Cloud Foundation (VCF), inherits Memory Tiering completely transparently, and what that means for your infrastructure consolidation strategy. Let’s dig in.

VKS – Kubernetes Built into VCF

VKS is a Cloud Native Computing Foundation (CNCF) conformant Kubernetes distribution that runs on top of the vSphere Supervisor. The Supervisor is the Kubernetes control plane embedded natively into each vSphere cluster, and is what enables VKS to provision and manage upstream Kubernetes clusters as first-class objects within VCF.

The same infrastructure policies, networking constructs, storage integrations, and lifecycle operations you rely on for your VMs apply equally to your Kubernetes clusters. There is no external Kubernetes management platform to stand up or maintain alongside your existing infrastructure stack, and no need to run a separate operational model for container workloads.

A few things that make VKS stand out in the VCF context.

  • Lifecycle management is automated. VKS cluster provisioning, upgrades, and scaling are managed natively through VCF. No separate lifecycle tooling is required.
  • Networking is integrated. VKS clusters use open-source CNI options (Antrea by default or Calico/Cilium). In NSX-enabled environments, VKS clusters leverage the same micro-segmentation, and policy controls your VMs already use.
  • Storage is native. Persistent volumes leverage vSAN and the broader VCF storage stack, with no bolt-on solutions required.
  • It’s included in VCF licensing. You’re not paying for a separate Kubernetes platform on top of your existing investment.

For organizations managing a mixed workload environment, VKS is the answer to the question of how to support containers without creating a second infrastructure silo. The result is a standards-conformant Kubernetes runtime with the operational consistency, storage, networking, and lifecycle integration of VCF built in.

And because VKS runs on the same vSphere infrastructure as your VMs, it also inherits every hypervisor-level capability automatically, including Memory Tiering.

Memory Tiering – What VKS Gets for Free

Memory Tiering isn’t something VKS workloads need to be configured to use. When you enable it on a VCF cluster, every workload running on that cluster benefits, whether it’s a traditional VM or a containerized application running inside a VKS-managed Kubernetes node.

Here’s how it works. vSphere manages a tiered memory pool that combines fast DRAM with a secondary tier, typically NVMe-based storage configured as a memory extension. The hypervisor handles the placement and movement of memory pages between tiers automatically, based on access patterns. Hot pages stay in DRAM. Cooler pages move to the secondary tier. If a cooled page gets accessed again, it’s promoted back. This entire process happens below the guest OS, below the Kubernetes node VM, and below the container runtime. Nothing above the hypervisor needs to know it’s happening.

There’s no driver to install, no kernel parameter to tune, and no application change required. The workload sees a single, contiguous memory address space, regardless of whether it’s a VM, a Kubernetes pod, or a containerized microservice. For VKS specifically, this means your platform team doesn’t need to manage memory tiering separately for container workloads. You configure it once at the cluster level, and VKS inherits it completely.

The practical implication is significant. You can run more VKS clusters per host, reduce the DRAM footprint required for your Kubernetes infrastructure, and drive down the cost per workload; all without touching application code, Kubernetes manifests, or container configurations. That’s a meaningful TCO lever, and it works across the entire VCF portfolio.

VKS and Memory Tiering 

A question people ask is whether their workloads running in VKS can benefit from Memory Tiering. We performed several experiments to answer this question using the popular HammerDB benchmark. We compared the relative throughput achieved by the benchmark between a Memory Tiering enabled system against a baseline where Memory Tiering is not enabled. The baseline cases ran on a host that has 1 TB of DRAM. The Memory Tiering cases ran on a host that has 512 GB of DRAM and 512 GB of Tier 1 memory from an NVMe SSD device.

Different HammerDB parameters were tested to demonstrate how VKS workloads can benefit from Memory Tiering. These test parameters change the working set exercised during the measurement while following the recommended guidelines for Memory Tiering, keeping the active memory under 50% of DRAM capacity. For further details on sizing guidance, refer to the Memory Tiering performance whitepaper. The chart below shows that our VKS workloads are able to achieve close to 100% of the throughput of the baseline, while running with only half the DRAM, using Memory Tiering. This is a significant infrastructure cost advantage offered by Memory Tiering.

We ran a similar set of tests to check the Memory Tiering benefits for VMs using the same HammerDB parameters. The table below shows that both VM and VKS workloads see similar infrastructure benefits, achieving throughput close to that of a fully DRAM-provisioned system, using only half the DRAM.

Test Parameters

All tests were run using HammerDB against MySQL, measuring Transactions Per Minute (TPM) across four virtual user (VU) concurrency levels, with the same infrastructure and Memory Tiering configuration for both environments.

Common parameters

  • MySQL innodb_buffer_pool_size set to 92GB
  • MySQL VM sized at 6 vCPUs + 120GB memory
  • HammerDB test with 25-minute ramp-up + 60-minute runtime

Bringing It All Together

Let’s step back and connect the dots, because this is where the VKS story gets really compelling.

VKS gives you a fully integrated, CNCF-conformant Kubernetes runtime inside VCF, without the operational overhead of a separate Kubernetes platform. And because it runs on the same vSphere infrastructure as your VMs, it inherits Memory Tiering automatically. No extra configuration, no separate capacity planning, no Kubernetes-specific memory policies to maintain.

What the test results confirm is that this inheritance is real and functionally complete. VKS workloads on Memory Tiering stay within 10% of a full DRAM baseline, matching what VMware documents for VM workloads. And when we run VKS and VMs side by side on the same Memory Tiering-enabled cluster, both showed clear benefits from memory tiering in a similar trend. 

What this means practically for your infrastructure planning.

  • VKS workloads can be sized and planned using the same Memory Tiering guidelines as VM workloads. One set of recommendations covers the entire VCF fleet.
  • TCO projections and consolidation ratios you’ve built for VM workloads translate to VKS workloads with confidence.
  • Teams running a hybrid of VMs and containers don’t need separate memory tiering policies, separate sizing guidance, or separate capacity plans. One VCF environment, one configuration, consistent results across both deployment models.

VKS in VCF already removes the operational tax of running Kubernetes alongside your VM infrastructure. Memory Tiering removes the DRAM tax of running it at scale. Together, they give you a genuinely unified platform for modern workloads, and the performance data backs it up.

Special Thanks

A big thank you to Ching-Yen, and Dazhi Wang for their contributions, testing work, and feedback that made this post possible.

item.content:encoded:
Learn how the VMware Aria Automation 8.18.1 to VCF Automation 9.1 upgrade works under the hood, covering the Fleet Lifecycle architecture, each migration phase, and exactly what happens to your data and services throughout the transition.

Overview

Upgrading from VMware Aria Automation 8.18.1 to VMware Cloud Foundation (VCF) Automation 9.1 is more than a version increment. The process introduces a carefully orchestrated migration architecture designed to safely transition your environment while preserving all existing automation content.

While the official upgrade guide covers each required step, this post explains the architecture behind the upgrade, the purpose of each migration stage, and what happens to your data and services throughout the process. Understanding this context will help you prepare more effectively for the transition.

Environment Details

This upgrade path applies to the following environment:

  • Source: VMware Aria Automation 8.18.x (minimum version 8.18.1)
  • Target: VCF Automation 9.1

Prerequisites

Ensure your environment meets the following requirements before initiating the upgrade through VCF Operations.

Technical Requirements:

  • Import: VMware Aria Automation 8.18.1 or later must be imported into VCF Operations.
  • Networking: Allocate a dedicated /29 CIDR block with a range of eight contiguous IP addresses for the cluster. Create a new VCF Services Runtime 9.1 FQDN that resolves to a unique IP address outside the dedicated CIDR range. This FQDN serves as the internal endpoint for the VCF Services runtime instance hosting the VCF Automation 9.1 nodes and is used exclusively for communication between VCF components.
  • Infrastructure: Download the VCF Automation 9.1.0.0 upgrade binaries and install the Migration Service Engine binary through the software depot.

The Fleet Lifecycle

The Fleet Lifecycle oversees the comprehensive lifecycle of management components, including end-to-end upgrades, patching, day-2 operations, and backup and recovery processes. It facilitates the transition to version 9.1.x for environments running VMware Aria Automation 8.18.x or VCF Automation 9.0.x.

Video walkthrough: A video overview of the Fleet Lifecycle upgrade process is available for reference.

Upgrade Process: Stage-by-Stage Breakdown

The transition from VMware Aria Automation 8.18.x to VCF Automation 9.1 follows a highly orchestrated workflow. The process divides into an initial import and orchestration phase, followed by a core 16-stage component upgrade.

Phase 1: Import and Orchestration

Before the upgrade begins, the Fleet Lifecycle collects the inputs needed to deploy the target environment. This top-level orchestration wrapper handles the following steps:

  1. Validation and Deployment: Validates all required configuration parameters and deploys the new VCF 9.1 service runtime and dedicated clusters as needed.
  2. Stage and Import: Stages the VCF Automation and bundle packages, then imports the existing VMware Aria Automation component to extract necessary details such as the component ID and sizing requirements.
  3. Pre-checks: Runs the comprehensive five-group pre-check sequence (connectivity, source, health, topology, application) against the target clusters.
  4. Trigger: Once the component is imported and validated, the Fleet Lifecycle initiates the core upgrade workflow on the cluster.

Phase 2: Preparation and Export (Stages 1 to 8)

In this phase, the source environment prepares for migration:

  1. Snapshots: Quiesced VM snapshots (without memory) are created through vCenter to provide a safe rollback point.
  2. Graceful Shutdowns: All pods and services on the source Aria Automation 8.18.x nodes are stopped via SSH.
  3. Data Export: The Aria Automation 8.18.x databases and configuration data are exported to “Hard disk 2”.
  4. All remaining internal pods and services are stopped, and the source VM name is stored securely.

Phase 3: The Downtime Window (Stages 9 to 12)

Downtime begins at Stage 9, when the original Aria Automation 8.18.x environment is powered off entirely. The Fleet Lifecycle then detaches “Hard disk 2” from the source node and mounts it to the target VCF Automation node.

Phase 4: Post-Deployment and Cleanup (Stages 13 to 16)

Once the new VCF Automation 9.1 cluster deploys successfully and begins serving traffic, the system initiates the post-deployment workflow:

  1. The system retrieves the original VM details and unmounts “Hard disk 2” from the new deployment, returning it to the original source VM.
  2. All temporary Kubernetes upgrade secrets are cleaned up to complete the process.

Summary

The orchestrated upgrade to VCF Automation 9.1 modernizes your infrastructure with minimal risk by isolating migration data onto a dedicated disk and transferring it cleanly to the new cluster. Each phase is designed to preserve your existing automation content while providing clear rollback options at every stage.

item.content:encoded:
Learn how the VCF Automation 9.0.x to 9.1.0.0 upgrade works, from the five precheck validation categories to the six-stage side-by-side migration model orchestrated by Fleet Lifecycle.

Overview

This post is part of the VCF Support infrastructure modernization series. It focuses exclusively on upgrading from VMware Cloud Foundation (VCF) Automation 9.0.x to 9.1.0.0, setting aside older 8.18.x migration paths to examine the current supported upgrade path in detail.

When planning a move to VCF Automation 9.1.0.0, preparation and predictability are critical. A successful upgrade depends on VCF’s Fleet Lifecycle management capabilities, and the central gatekeeper to this entire process is the Precheck Phase. This post explains what occurs during these prechecks and maps out the execution stages the system proceeds through to complete the upgrade.

Video walkthrough: A video overview of the Fleet Lifecycle upgrade process is available for reference.

Environment Details

  • Source version: VCF Automation 9.0.x
  • Target version: VCF Automation 9.1.0.0

Prerequisites

Before initiating the upgrade, confirm the following:

  • The source appliance is running a supported VCF Automation 9.0.x build.
  • The Primary FQDN resolves correctly to an IP address.
  • SSH (port 22) is accessible and authentication is configured.
  • Kubernetes nodes are in a “Ready” state.
  • Sufficient disk I/O capacity is available on Postgres pods. This is validated by a 30-second, 250 MB latency test during prechecks.
  • DNS resolves correctly for all allocated node IPs.
  • Allocated node IPs are not already in use on the network.

Understanding the Precheck Phase

Upgrading an automation platform requires orchestrating new configurations and migrating data at scale. The precheck phase serves as a non-destructive safety net, running a series of validations in a strict dependency order before any destructive operations are triggered.

The Five Precheck Categories

The Fleet Lifecycle evaluates the environment across five major categories to confirm readiness before the upgrade begins:

  • Connectivity Checks: The Fleet Lifecycle verifies communication channels with the source environment. This includes confirming that the Primary FQDN resolves to an IP address, verifying that SSH (port 22) is open, ensuring cipher negotiation matches expectations, and validating SSH authentication.
  • Source Validation: The system verifies that the upgrade proceeds from a supported starting point. It runs a Product Identification Check to confirm the source is a VCF Automation 9.0.x product, alongside a strict Version Validation Check.
  • Health Checks: The system confirms that Kubernetes nodes are in a “Ready” state, verifies that application category services are healthy, checks for database split-brain conditions, validates the TLS certificate chain, and runs a 30-second, 250 MB disk I/O latency test on Postgres pods.
  • Topology Checks: This phase confirms that the physical and logical infrastructure maps correctly to the upgrade configuration. It validates datastore consistency, checks that node IP pools and Platform VIPs fall within the target network CIDR block, confirms DNS resolution locally, and pings allocated node IPs to verify they are not already in use.
  • Application Prechecks: The system verifies application-level compliance, specifically the FIPS Endpoint Compatibility check, which assesses the current FIPS mode status on the source VCF Automation 9.x environment.

Troubleshooting note: If a precheck fails, the 9.x precheck execution logs are written via SSH to the source appliance at the following path:

“/tmp/vcfa-upgrade/logs/upgrade-precheck<script> <timestamp>.log”

Executing the VCF Automation 9.1 Upgrade

VCF Automation does not perform an in-place software update. Instead, it uses a side-by-side migration approach. The Fleet Lifecycle deploys a new 9.1 cluster alongside the existing 9.0.x nodes, migrates data to the new cluster, and then powers down the legacy environment. This approach reduces risk and preserves data integrity throughout the transition.

The Complete Upgrade Workflow

The upgrade process proceeds through six coordinated stages:

Stage 1: Initialization and Staging
The system retrieves source component details, initializes required parameters, and validates the IP and FQDN specifications provided during configuration. It then stages the necessary VCF Automation packages and imports the source configuration.

Stage 2: Create Automation Cluster
The Fleet Lifecycle creates a dedicated vcf-automation folder on the management vCenter, deploys a runtime template (vcf-services-runtime-template-9.1.0.0), and provisions a temporary bootstrap virtual machine. The bootstrap VM clones and deploys three new VCF Automation 9.1 nodes, assigning them IP addresses from the provided CIDR block.

Stage 3: Discover Automation Cluster
Once the new virtual machines are online, an initialization process discovers the newly created VCF services runtime cluster and verifies it is ready to receive data.

Stage 4: Perform Component Upgrade
This is the core data migration phase. The orchestrator syncs legacy 9.0.x data to the new 9.1 nodes through the following sequence:

  1. A full backup of the source 9.0.x cluster is initiated.
  2. The Postgres database is prepared for migration.
  3. VCF component services on the source cluster are scaled down to prevent new writes.
  4. A final component backup is taken and data is transferred to the new cluster.
  5. Services and configurations are restored on the target 9.1 nodes.
  6. The old 9.0.x nodes are powered off.
  7. Component services are installed on the new cluster, the Postgres upgrade is finalized, and the target component version is patched to 9.1.0.0.

Stage 5: Install Backend Services
The system installs the required VCD Migrator Backend Service on the new 9.1 cluster.

Stage 6: Inventory Sync and Cleanup
The Fleet Lifecycle runs an inventory sync to register the new 9.1 infrastructure in the Fleet Lifecycle manager. It then unstages downloaded binaries and removes all temporary files.

Summary

The upgrade from VCF Automation 9.0.x to 9.1 is designed to be automated and low-risk. The precheck phase validates network topology, credentials, and database performance before any configuration changes occur. The side-by-side migration model ensures continuity by standing up the new environment before decommissioning the old one. Understanding these validation gates and execution stages enables administrators to plan and execute infrastructure modernization with confidence.

Acknowledgements

Special thanks to Arun Nukula, Iyaz Khan, and Owen Sheehy.

item.content:encoded:
Nothing marks the start of quite Explore like the Hands-on Labs Command Center Wall!

Weeks before Explore happens, a small team of dedicated engineers begins designing and building the infrastructure monitoring.  The dashboards created are then used to populate the Command Center Wall – these live dashboards monitor the usage, metrics and performance of the infrastructure – in real time!  When you sit down to take a lab, your impact shows up on the wall! 

This year, the Command Center Wall is showcasing the full power of VCF 9.1 – and there’s a lot to showcase.

A Living Dashboard for a Live Event

The Command Center Wall isn’t just eye candy. Every metric on those displays is pulling live data from the actual Hands-on Labs production environment. What you see is what’s real – if a host goes red, you’re seeing the actual state of the infrastructure. No smoke and mirrors, no synthetic data. Full transparency, live and at scale.

The team behind the wall begins building well before the doors open. Dashboards are architected, tuned, and sometimes built on-site during setup days to make sure everything tells the right story at the right scale. That flexibility – the ability to spin up or modify a dashboard on the fly to meet the demands of a live event – is exactly what the VCF 9.1 platform is designed to enable. It’s the kind of thing you can only appreciate when you’re watching it happen in a real production environment.

VCF 9.1 Takes Center Stage

This year the monitoring is showcasing VCF 9.1 across its full stack. Here’s what’s coming:

VCF Operations has been a staple of the Command Center Wall for several years, and 9.1 brings improvements to dashboards, data presentation, and customization that make it easier to surface the right metrics at the right time. Custom dashboards tailored to the event environment span partner cloud capacity, private cloud hosts, and everything in between – a showcase of just how flexible the platform is.

VCF Operations for Logs is now deeply integrated into the core Operations experience in 9.1, and the CCW puts that integration front and center. A dedicated Logs dashboard built specifically for the Command Center Wall surfaces log insights in a way that’s both visually compelling and operationally actionable – even for first-time viewers.

VCF Operations for Networks rounds out the observability story. At a conference of this scale, network visibility isn’t optional – it’s critical. Operations for Networks delivers end-to-end topology and performance insight, all feeding into the same monitoring fabric that powers the wall.

VCF Telemetry feeds the entire observability pipeline, collecting and forwarding the metrics and signals that everything else depends on. It’s the connective tissue that makes the rest of the stack coherent — the layer you don’t notice until it’s not there.

Newly added for this year are SSP and Memory Tiering:

Security Services Platform (SSP) brings the advanced security services layer of vDefend 9.1 to the Command Center Wall. SSP is integrated with NSX and hosts and manages a suite of security capabilities. These capabilities include Security Intelligence for distributed visibility, traffic flow analysis, and micro-segmentation policy recommendations; Network Detection and Response (NDR) for continuous threat monitoring using IDS/IPS and advanced threat analysis; Malware Prevention Service for file-level protection against known and zero-day threats; and Network Traffic Analysis for identifying anomalies and suspicious behavior across the network. Rounding it out is the Metrics feature, which collects point-in-time and time-series data.. At Explore, those metrics are feeding directly into the live dashboards on the wall – giving the Security Services Platform a natural home on the Command Center Wall display.

Memory Tiering is one of the more technically compelling additions in 9.1. By extending memory capacity across tiered storage, it allows the Hands-on Labs monitoring infrastructure to do more with the same physical footprint.

Come See It for Yourself

The Command Center Wall is worth a few minutes of your time at Explore. Stop by, take in the dashboards, and ask questions. The team that built it is there and happy to talk through what you’re seeing. It’s a rare opportunity to see an enterprise-scale VCF 9.1 deployment doing real work, in real time, at a real event.

See you at the wall.
